sources.context: Vogue’s October 2026 cover story, reported over a July 2026 afternoon at Johnson’s new Los Angeles house and timed to the October 2, 2026 release of Verity. A cover story is a negotiated, promotional encounter; the writer frames Johnson against her reputation for “cool-girl deadpan opacity.” It is the most recent long-form first-person record and includes named friends and colleagues (logged separately as S18–S22). The writer, not Johnson, supplies the Ellen paraphrase, the lime-allergy aside and the detail about a teacher reading a tabloid. It also dates the end of her eight-year partnership with Chris Martin to June 2025 and records her declining to discuss her current romantic status.

claims.claim: The Vogue writer records that suggesting passion clashed with her “cool remove” was the first time she saw Johnson’s “feathers ruffle.”
claims.passage: records the first time its writer, Alessandra Codinha, saw "her feathers ruffle." Codinha had wondered whether "no-holds-barred passion goes against that image of her cool remove."
claims.inference: An outside observer marks this as the one point of visible irritation in the interview.
claims.alternative: The writer’s framing in a promotional cover story; she chose what to report.

claims.claim: Johnson answered: “No. I deeply care… I wouldn’t say that I’m cool. What is that, even?… I just want to be authentic.”
claims.passage: Johnson answered: "No. I deeply care about a lot of things. I *deeply* care. I wouldn't say that I'm cool. What *is* that, even?" Then, "plainly": "I just want to be authentic."
claims.inference: What provokes her is being misidentified, not being challenged.
claims.alternative: Anyone might bristle at a reductive label in a cover interview, and resisting “cool” is also good image management.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the lie costs her nothing while the label does.
claims.passage: So here is a woman who, by Vogue's account, will cheerfully lie about fruit, and who bristles at being called cool. The likeliest explanation is that the lie costs her nothing while the label does.
claims.inference: Built from C12 and C14; labeled as the likeliest explanation.
claims.alternative: She may simply enjoy mischief (see C117), or the bristling may be momentary.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Johnson’s most consistent motive across 2015–2026 is to be met as she actually is, felt and specific, rather than as an image someone else shaped. That best fits Type 4.
claims.passage: Across a decade of interviews, what she protects most is being met as she actually is, felt and specific, rather than as an image someone else shaped.
claims.inference: Built from C14–C19, C24–C26, C36, C61 and C72. Medium confidence: the motive repeats across press, work and relationships and outside witnesses corroborate it, but much of the record is promotional self-description.
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Six is the strongest rival (C20–C23, C90–C92); Eight and Nine explain parts of the persona (C13, C34, C98; C29, C32).

claims.claim: Interpretation stated in the opening: she plays with facts that do not define her and pushes back when her self or work gets turned into something else.
claims.passage: She plays with facts that do not define her, and she pushes back when her self or her work gets turned into something else.
claims.inference: Thesis drawn from C11, C12, C14, C25, C64–C66 and C09.
claims.alternative: The trivia/identity line is the profile’s interpretation; the article says so in C117.

claims.claim: She returns to difference and authenticity across years: 2017 “different is what I’m about”; 2026 “I just want to be authentic.”
claims.passage: In 2017 she said of *Fifty Shades*, "different is what I'm about." In 2026 she said, "I just want to be authentic."
claims.inference: A stable organizing value across nine years.
claims.alternative: “Authentic” is common indie-actor and brand vocabulary; her put-ons (C11) and years of on-message promotion (C101) show she performs when she judges it necessary.

claims.claim: She told Bustle in 2024 that she had exaggerated in the interview and that written text loses her tone.

claims.inference: A caveat she supplies on her own quotes; the draft applies it to all quotes.
claims.alternative: None; it limits the weight of individual lines.

claims.claim: Vogue (2017) describes her as raised “nowhere in particular,” traveling with nannies and tutors, unable to count her schools, and in therapy from age three.

claims.inference: Context for lifelong rootlessness; not proof of type.
claims.alternative: Any child raised this way could feel unanchored (C57 tempers the hardship reading).

claims.passage: Vogue also noted her parents' divorce and "their well-publicized struggles with drugs and alcohol."
claims.inference: A concrete, non-typological reason for her guardedness about privacy.
claims.alternative: Sensitive family material; the draft uses only Vogue’s already-published phrasing and builds no causal childhood-wound argument on it.

claims.passage: Her summary: "I was so consistently unmoored and discombobulated. I didn't have an anchor anywhere."
claims.inference: Her own account of rootlessness.
claims.alternative: Circumstance explains it fully.

claims.passage: In 2024 she said of the constant moving, "I didn't find it weird because it was what was normal to me"
claims.inference: Tempers the hardship reading; she resists a purely tragic version too.

claims.inference: Recasts difference as something understood rather than fixed.

claims.passage: asked about a novel whose narrator believes she is an alien, she said: "I don't know if I'm from anywhere or I belong anywhere. So, yes, I do relate to the alien."
claims.inference: A recurrent self-concept of outsiderness, typical of the Four’s focus on what sets the self apart.
claims.alternative: Her nomadic childhood (C02) fully explains feeling from nowhere.

claims.claim: Interpretation: she treats her difference as something to be understood and later as a value.
claims.passage: She treats her difference as something to be understood, and later as a value, more than as a problem to fix.
claims.inference: Built from C59, C15 and C17.
claims.alternative: A reading of self-report; others with the same childhood might say the same.

claims.claim: Across 2020–2025 she describes the same grievance in nearly the same words: a project became a different thing from what she signed up for.

claims.inference: Four dated statements (C25, C64, C65, C66) share one structure. This repeated phrasing is the profile’s central observed pattern.
claims.alternative: Common actor complaint about studio films; each instance was prompted by an interviewer.

claims.claim: In February 2020, explaining why she started TeaTime, she told Marie Claire she would “do a movie and have no say… it comes out as a totally different thing.”
claims.passage: In February 2020, explaining why she started TeaTime, she told Marie Claire: "For a long time, I'd do a movie and have no say. I could go into something, and it'll be one thing, and then it comes out as a totally different thing. As an artist, you're like, 'What the fuck?'"
claims.inference: She answered the loss of voice by building a vehicle for her own taste.
claims.alternative: An Eight reading sees a control move; also a common career step. Marie Claire notes she had denied reports of displeasure with Fifty Shades.

claims.inference: Fourth instance of the pattern.

claims.passage: In 2022 she told Vanity Fair that the author, E.L. James, "had a lot of creative control, all day, every day," and that "It was always a battle. Always." She and Jamie Dornan, she said, would shoot "the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then we would do the takes of the movie that we wanted to make," and she would rewrite scenes the night before.
claims.inference: Her grievance is that the work became something other than what she signed up for; her response was a workaround plus years of discretion.
claims.alternative: Johnson’s account of a named living person; no public response from James was opened. She blames a “Combo” of studio, directors and author.
claims.review_trigger: If E.L. James, the studio or another named participant responds publicly to Johnson’s 2022 account.

claims.claim: She said knowing in advance would have been “psychotic” but does not regret it, called James “a very nice woman” who “was always kind to me,” and blamed a “Combo.”
claims.passage: Had she known what it would be like, she said, "It would've been like, 'Oh, this is psychotic.' But no, I don't regret it." She also called James "a very nice woman" who "was always kind to me." The account is Johnson's, given seven years after the first film, and she blamed a "Combo" of studio, directors and author.
claims.inference: Balances the grievance with praise and no regret; attribution kept explicit.
claims.alternative: Diplomatic phrasing about a collaborator is also career-prudent.

claims.alternative: Contradicted in part by her put-ons (C11) and on-message promotion (C101).

claims.inference: Public put-ons defend a private self.
claims.alternative: Sits awkwardly beside her authenticity creed and fits a playful Seven or combative Eight as easily.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 4. (1) Anxiety and vigilance run through the record: “the most insane anxiety” that keeps her up “all night, every night” (C21), a “K-hole of feeling so scared of people” (C90), the sense that “everyone is a spy” (C91), constant safety language (C20, C92), loyalty to chosen family (C23), the cult/defiance ambivalence (C22) and “How could you not have warned us?” (C38). The counterphobic Six case is substantial. (2) The persona reads as Eight: “a very defiant person” who finds rules “ridiculous” (C13), corrected Ellen DeGeneres on air (C09, C78), messes with the press “because the other side is fucking with me” (C77), founded a company so she would have a say (C25, C71), and costars describe “takes no prisoners” and “jungle cat energy” (C34, C98). (3) Nine-like going-along and withdrawal (C29, C32). type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Counterphobic Type 6 is the strongest rival. She reports chronic anxiety and fear (C21, C90, C91), uses “safe,” “protected” and “protect” repeatedly (C20, C92, C26), values loyalty to a chosen circle over blood (C23), distrusts executives and the press (C30, C77), and shows a split relation to authority in one exchange: “the first one to join a cult” yet “a very defiant person” left “shaking” when told she can’t (C22). Her protectiveness toward her grandmother (C38) and closing up “when I don’t feel protected” (C20) fit a security-driven core whose fear comes out as provocation. Type 8 is the second rival (C09, C13, C25, C34, C98); Type 9 explains withdrawal and “along for the ride” (C29, C32); Type 7 explains mischief and silliness (C11, C33) but not her dwelling in pain (C18, C87).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What her safety is for, and what her grievances are about. A Six tends to treat safety and certainty as the goal and to lean on method, preparation or trusted guidance when anxious. Johnson frames safety as what releases expression: “when I feel safe, I think I can do anything” (2017) and “When people feel valued and safe to explore their minds, magic happens” (2026) (C94); even “a little bit more safe” came with wanting to keep believing in the Easter Bunny (C95). She rejects method and structure (C24, C13). Her repeated grievance, in nearly the same words in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, is that a project became “a totally different thing” from what she signed up for (C61, C25, C64, C65, C66, C69), while transformation she chooses she welcomes (C72, C19). The one moment Vogue saw her bristle was being called cool, answered with “I just want to be authentic” (C49, C14). When low she reaches for meaning (C04, C88, C96). Against Eight: volunteered vulnerability across nine years (C35, C87, C99) and described ceding control (C29). Against Nine: she keeps asserting her own taste (C70). The discriminator rests largely on self-report in promotional interviews, hence medium confidence.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Her relish for public put-ons (“The most fun”; the AD limes) in someone whose stated creed is authenticity (C11, C12, C117); the reversal from “probably will never do anything like it again” (March 2024) to “There’s no part of me that’s like, ‘Oh, I’ll never do that again’” (June 2025) (C28); years of on-message Fifty Shades promotion before saying she could not speak “truthfully” (C101, C08); the slapstick sociability friends describe (C33); deliberate commercial trade-offs (“this is a business,” C39); and an anxiety level high for a Four that may reflect depression, circumstance or a Six core (C102). Whether her defiance is temperament or a learned response to a childhood lived in public remains open.
